title: Day one, six months, or still two years?
subtitle: The Employment Rights Act 2025 layered onto the current unfair dismissal scheme
objectives: Identify which Employment Rights Act 2025 reforms are already in force (trade union recognition and access, from 6 April 2026 and 30 October 2026) versus which are enacted but not yet commenced (the unfair dismissal qualifying period, dismissal-and-rehire, guaranteed hours)

State the current, in-force unfair dismissal qualifying period under ss 94–98 ERA 1996, and explain how the ERA 2025 is set to reduce it to six months from 1 January 2027 — and why that is different from the 'day one' right first proposed

Explain the practical significance of dismissal-and-rehire becoming automatically unfair in most cases, and of the new right to guaranteed hours for zero-hours workers, including why their commencement dates are still provisional

leadingAuthorities.role: The reforming Act — Royal Assent obtained in 2025, with implementation phased through 2027
The comparator: the current, in-force law on the right not to be unfairly dismissed and the existing qualifying period

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson sits apart from the rest of the module: it teaches law that has received Royal Assent but, for its headline unfair dismissal reforms, has not yet commenced. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You've heard the headlines — this lesson checks whether you know which ones are actually in force yet.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards 'is this in force today' scenario questions, dated relative to 1 January 2027 — expect to work out which regime applies to a dismissal on a specific date, not just recite the headline figures.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the distinction between Royal Assent and commencement is the foundation the rest of this lesson, and every fact pattern in its test pool, depends on.

overview.hook: A headline in 2024 announces 'unfair dismissal protection from day one'. Eighteen months later, the Act that actually receives Royal Assent gives workers a six-month qualifying period instead — a real cut from the current two years, but not the day-one right the same government first proposed. Neither headline was wrong exactly; they were snapshots of a law still being built in public, one amendment and one commencement regulation at a time. This lesson teaches you to tell the difference between what Parliament has enacted and what is actually, today, the law that governs a dismissal.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. This lesson is the single biggest currency risk in the Employment law module: the Employment Rights Act 2025 received Royal Assent in 2025, but almost none of its central unfair dismissal and fire-and-rehire reforms are in force yet. They are currently scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027, and even that roadmap has already shifted once — from an original 'day one' unfair dismissal right to the six-month qualifying period now provided for. The trade union recognition and access reforms are a partial exception: those provisions are already in force, from 6 April 2026 and 30 October 2026. Before relying on this lesson, `lawStatedAt` should be checked against the government's and ACAS's implementation trackers — secondary legislation and codes of practice were still being published through 2026–2027 as at the check date, and commencement dates in this area have already moved once before.

parts.heading: Enacted is not the same as in force
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Royal Assent tells you Parliament has finished with a Bill. It does not, by itself, tell you the Act is actually operating law that a court or tribunal will apply. Most Acts — and the Employment Rights Act 2025 is a clean example — bring their provisions into force in stages, through separate commencement regulations, often months or years after Royal Assent.

This matters enormously for this lesson because the ERA 2025 is not one single change on one single date. Different provisions commence on different dates, some already passed, most still ahead. Treating 'the Employment Rights Act 2025 has received Royal Assent' as equivalent to 'the Employment Rights Act 2025 is the law today' is the single most common error this topic produces — and it is precisely the error every scenario in this lesson's test pool is built to catch.

Contrast this with the automatically unfair dismissal categories from lesson 7 (whistleblowing, pregnancy, trade union membership, asserting a statutory right) — those are current, fully in-force law today, with no qualifying period, and nothing in this lesson changes that. What this lesson adds is a second, prospective layer: reforms that will, on current plans, become law on top of the scheme in lessons 5–8, not instead of it — yet.

components.label: What's actually happening, and when
points: Trade union recognition and access reforms — already in force, from 6 April 2026 and 30 October 2026
Unfair dismissal qualifying period cut to six months — enacted, but not commenced; expected 1 January 2027
Dismissal-and-rehire restriction (automatically unfair in most cases) — enacted, but not commenced; expected 1 January 2027
Zero-hours guaranteed hours right — enacted, but not commenced; implementation date not yet fixed, expected 2027

interaction.prompt: Is the Employment Rights Act 2025 the law currently governing the unfair dismissal qualifying period, as at the law-stated date of this lesson?
options: No — the current law is still ss 94–98 ERA 1996's two-year qualifying period; the ERA 2025's six-month threshold is not yet commenced
Yes — the ERA 2025 replaced the two-year rule the moment it received Royal Assent
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Royal Assent is not commencement. Until the relevant commencement regulations take effect — currently expected 1 January 2027 — the existing two-year qualifying period under ss 94–98 ERA 1996 remains the operative law.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not yet — Royal Assent only means Parliament has finished the Bill. The ERA 2025's unfair dismissal reforms are scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027; until then, the current two-year qualifying period under ss 94–98 ERA 1996 still applies.

parts.heading: The current scheme it's replacing: the two-year qualifying period
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: To understand what's changing, you need the current rule firmly in view — this is the comparator law, still fully in force, that lessons 5 to 8 teach in depth and that this lesson assumes as background.

s 108(1) ERA 1996 provides that the general right not to be unfairly dismissed under s 94 does not apply unless the employee has been continuously employed for a period of not less than two years ending with the effective date of termination. That is the qualifying period students have to apply today, and will continue to have to apply to any dismissal that takes place before the ERA 2025's threshold change actually commences.

Within that two-year framework, the employer must still show one of the five potentially fair reasons (conduct, capability, redundancy, illegality, or some other substantial reason — lesson 5), and the dismissal must satisfy the Burchell test and the range of reasonable responses standard (lesson 6). None of that machinery is touched by the ERA 2025 reforms covered in this lesson; what changes, eventually, is simply which employees are eligible to bring the claim in the first place.

components.text: Section 94 does not apply to the dismissal of an employee unless he has been continuously employed for a period of not less than two years ending with the effective date of termination.
elements: Currently in force — this is today's law
Two years' continuous employment, ending with the effective date of termination
Applies to the general s 94 right; the automatically unfair categories in lesson 7 are unaffected and need no qualifying period

interaction.prompt: As at the law-stated date of this lesson, an employee with 14 months' continuous service is dismissed for an ordinary conduct reason, with no automatically unfair factor in play. Can she bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim under s 94?
options: No — s 108(1) currently requires two years' continuous service, and 14 months falls short
Yes — the ERA 2025's six-month threshold already governs her dismissal
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Until the ERA 2025's threshold change commences, s 108(1)'s two-year requirement is still the operative law, so 14 months' service is not enough for an ordinary unfair dismissal claim.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The ERA 2025's six-month threshold is not yet in force — s 108(1)'s current two-year requirement still governs a dismissal today, and 14 months does not satisfy it.

parts.heading: From 'day one' to six months: how the roadmap moved
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strongest case for the rule, then complicates it
body: The Employment Rights Bill, as first introduced, proposed removing the qualifying period for unfair dismissal altogether — a 'day one' right, available from an employee's first day in a job, albeit expected to come with some form of lighter-touch dismissal process available to employers during an initial period of employment.

That proposal met sustained pushback during consultation, largely from employer groups warning about the practical difficulty of managing probationary hiring decisions if every new hire carried full unfair dismissal exposure from day one. The Bill was amended before passage, and the Act that actually received Royal Assent — the Employment Rights Act 2025 — instead provides for a six-month qualifying period, not a day-one right.

Six months is still a substantial cut from the current two years, and represents a genuine, significant change to employer risk in the first year of a hire. But it is not what the original headlines promised, and a student who answers 'day one' when asked what the ERA 2025 actually provides is answering the wrong Bill, not the wrong Act — the distinction between the original proposal and the enacted version is itself testable.

This threshold change, like dismissal-and-rehire in Part 4, is currently scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027 — a date fixed by government announcement and commencement regulations rather than by the Act's own text, meaning it remains, in principle, capable of being moved again before it takes effect.

components.definition: Currently two years under s 108(1) ERA 1996, in force today. The Employment Rights Act 2025 reduces this to six months — not the 'day one' right originally proposed — but that change is not yet in force; it is currently scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened (or are currently scheduled to happen).
items: The Employment Rights Bill is introduced, proposing a 'day one' unfair dismissal right
Consultation raises employer concerns about day-one exposure for new hires
The Bill is amended to provide a six-month qualifying period instead of day one
The Employment Rights Act 2025 receives Royal Assent
The six-month qualifying period is currently scheduled to commence, on 1 January 2027
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the arc: an ambitious day-one proposal, consultation pushback, a scaled-back enacted version, Royal Assent — and still a further wait for commencement. Every stage matters for knowing what the law actually is on any given date.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again: the day-one proposal came first, consultation narrowed it to six months before the Bill passed, Royal Assent followed, and commencement — the point the change actually takes effect — is scheduled later still, for 1 January 2027.

parts.heading: Dismissal-and-rehire becomes automatically unfair (from 1 January 2027)
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: Today, 'fire and rehire' — dismissing an employee and immediately re-engaging them on less favourable terms, typically to force through a contract variation the employee won't agree to — is not automatically unfair. It is simply tested under the ordinary unfair dismissal framework from lessons 5 and 6: the employer needs a potentially fair reason (usually 'some other substantial reason') and a reasonable process, and tribunals have historically given employers real latitude here, particularly where there's a genuine business rationale.

The practice attracted sustained public and political criticism following high-profile cases of large-scale fire-and-rehire being used to cut costs, most notably in the shipping and logistics sector. The ERA 2025 responds by making dismissal for refusing to agree a contract variation automatically unfair in most cases, subject to narrow exceptions — broadly, where the employer can show genuine financial difficulties that threaten the survival of the business and no reasonable alternative course of action was available.

Like the qualifying period change, this reform is enacted but not yet in force. It is currently scheduled to commence alongside the six-month qualifying period, on 1 January 2027. Until that date, a fire-and-rehire dismissal remains governed entirely by the ordinary unfair dismissal test — it is not automatically unfair today, however politically controversial the practice has become.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that because fire-and-rehire has been so heavily criticised in the media and in Parliament, it must already be automatically unfair under current law.
components.whyItsWrong: Political controversy and legislative reform are not the same as commencement. As at the law-stated date of this lesson, dismissal-and-rehire is still assessed under the ordinary potentially-fair-reason and reasonableness framework from lessons 5 and 6. The ERA 2025's automatic unfairness rule for this practice does not take effect until the relevant commencement regulations bring it into force, currently expected 1 January 2027.

interaction.prompt: As at the law-stated date of this lesson, is dismissing and re-engaging an employee on worse terms ('fire and rehire') automatically unfair?
options: No — it is currently assessed under the ordinary unfair dismissal test; automatic unfairness under the ERA 2025 is not yet in force
Yes — the ERA 2025 made this automatically unfair the moment it received Royal Assent
No — fire and rehire has always been, and remains, entirely lawful with no restriction at all
interaction.trapExplanation: The second option confuses Royal Assent with commencement — the automatic unfairness reform is not yet in force. The third option overcorrects: fire and rehire is not automatically unfair today, but it has always still needed to satisfy the ordinary unfair dismissal test (a potentially fair reason and a reasonable process) — it has never been unrestricted.

parts.heading: Guaranteed hours, and the exception that's already live
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in the syllabus
body: The ERA 2025 also gives zero-hours and low-hours workers a new right to guaranteed hours, reflecting the hours they actually, regularly work over a reference period — aimed at ending the practice of employers keeping staff on paper zero-hours contracts while relying on them for a genuinely predictable weekly rota. As with the two reforms already covered, this right is enacted but not yet in force: its precise implementation date has not been fixed, and is currently expected sometime in 2027.

It's worth closing on the one part of this reform wave that breaks the pattern, because it is exactly the kind of fact a well-set exam question will test: the ERA 2025's trade union recognition and access reforms are not still waiting for a future commencement date — they are already in force, having commenced on 6 April 2026 and 30 October 2026 respectively. If a scenario asks whether a trade union can currently rely on statutory access rights under the ERA 2025, the answer, unlike almost everything else in this lesson, is yes.

The single skill this lesson is really testing, across every fact pattern in its test pool, is date discipline: identify the date on the facts, identify which specific ERA 2025 provision is engaged, and check whether that specific provision's commencement date has actually arrived — never assume the whole Act moves as one block.

components.definition: A right for zero-hours and low-hours workers under the Employment Rights Act 2025 to be offered guaranteed hours reflecting hours regularly worked over a reference period. Enacted but not yet in force; implementation date not yet fixed, expected during 2027.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the Employment Rights Act 2025's trade union recognition and access reforms are already in force, as at the law-stated date of this lesson?
interaction.explanation: Already in force — unlike the qualifying period, fire-and-rehire and guaranteed hours reforms, the trade union recognition and access provisions commenced on 6 April 2026 and 30 October 2026. This is the exception in this lesson's pattern, and exactly the kind of distinction a scenario question will test.

testPool.prompt: State the qualifying period for unfair dismissal under the current, in-force law (ss 94–98 ERA 1996), as it stands today.
testPool.modelAnswer: Two years' continuous employment, ending with the effective date of termination, under s 108(1) ERA 1996 — this remains the current law until the ERA 2025's six-month threshold commences.

testPool.prompt: State the date on which the Employment Rights Act 2025's six-month unfair dismissal qualifying period is currently scheduled to commence.
testPool.modelAnswer: 1 January 2027 — currently scheduled, but not guaranteed, since the roadmap for this reform has already shifted once before (from a 'day one' right to six months).

testPool.prompt: Are the Employment Rights Act 2025's trade union recognition and access reforms already in force, as at the law-stated date of this lesson?
Which of the following dismissals could an employee with 14 months' service NOT bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim for today, given the current law, absent an automatically unfair reason?
options: A dismissal for an ordinary conduct reason, because 14 months is below the current two-year qualifying period
A dismissal connected with whistleblowing, because that requires no qualifying period under s 103A
A dismissal connected with pregnancy, because that requires no qualifying period

testPool.prompt: Order these events in the legislative roadmap for the ERA 2025's unfair dismissal reform.
items: The Employment Rights Bill is published, containing a 'day one' unfair dismissal proposal
Employer groups raise concerns during consultation about day-one exposure for new hires
The Bill passes with a six-month qualifying period instead of a day-one right
The Employment Rights Act 2025 receives Royal Assent
Commencement regulations are expected to bring the six-month threshold into force on 1 January 2027

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate description of the ERA 2025's unfair dismissal reform as actually enacted?
options: A reduction of the qualifying period from two years to six months, currently scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027
A 'day one' right to claim unfair dismissal from the first day of employment
No change at all to the qualifying period — the reform only concerns trade unions
testPool.trapExplanation: Many students recall the original 'day one' headline rather than what was actually enacted after consultation — the second option describes the abandoned proposal, not the Act. The third option is also wrong: the qualifying period reform is real and substantial, just not yet in force.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that dismissal-and-rehire ('fire and rehire') is automatically unfair under the law as it stands today?
sliderLabels: Not yet — still governed by the ordinary unfair dismissal test
testPool.correctPosition: not yet — still governed by the ordinary unfair dismissal test
testPool.explanation: Not yet. The ERA 2025's rule making fire-and-rehire automatically unfair in most cases is enacted but not commenced, currently scheduled for 1 January 2027. Today, it is still assessed under the ordinary potentially-fair-reason and reasonableness framework.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact most relevant to whether this dismissal might fall within the ERA 2025's narrow exception for fire-and-rehire, once that reform is in force.
testPool.scenarioText: In March 2028, a manufacturer facing genuine, well-evidenced insolvency risk consults staff, explores every alternative it can identify, and finally dismisses and re-engages its workforce on reduced terms because there is no other way to keep the business trading.
tappableSpans: explores every alternative it can identify
dismisses and re-engages its workforce on reduced terms
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the fact the narrow exception turns on. The ERA 2025's exception is aimed at employers facing genuine financial difficulties threatening the survival of the business with no reasonable alternative — insolvency risk of this kind is exactly the scenario it's designed to accommodate, unlike a routine cost-cutting exercise.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Consultation and exploring alternatives matter to the ordinary fairness of the process, but the exception itself turns on the underlying reason — genuine financial difficulty threatening the business's survival — being the reason for using fire-and-rehire at all.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that determines which qualifying-period regime governs this employee's potential claim.
testPool.scenarioText: An employee with nine months' service is dismissed for a conduct reason on 15 December 2026. She wants to know whether she can bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim.
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. The date of dismissal is what matters — 15 December 2026 falls before the ERA 2025's six-month threshold is scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027, so the current two-year qualifying period under s 108(1) still governs her dismissal, and nine months' service is not enough.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Her length of service and the reason for dismissal matter to the underlying claim, but the fact that decides which regime applies at all is the date of dismissal relative to the ERA 2025's scheduled commencement date.

testPool.prompt: Aisha has worked for her employer for 18 months. In November 2026 she is dismissed after refusing to accept a unilateral pay cut, and is not re-engaged on any terms. She asks whether she can bring an unfair dismissal claim today, and whether her answer would be any different if the same dismissal happened in February 2027 instead.
factsToOrder: She is dismissed in November 2026 for refusing a unilateral pay cut
The ERA 2025's six-month qualifying period is not yet in force in November 2026
By February 2027, the ERA 2025's six-month threshold is scheduled to be in force

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Aisha can bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim, applying the qualifying period in force on the date of her dismissal, and whether the answer changes if the dismissal is instead dated after the ERA 2025's threshold change commences.
modelAnswer.rule: The current qualifying period is two years under s 108(1) ERA 1996. The ERA 2025 reduces this to six months, but that change is not yet in force and is currently scheduled to commence on 1 January 2027. Which regime applies turns on the date of dismissal, not the date the claim is assessed.
modelAnswer.application: On the November 2026 facts, Aisha has 18 months' service, which satisfies neither the current two-year requirement nor (if it were already in force) the future six-month threshold in a way that changes the outcome, since 18 months exceeds six months in any event — but crucially, in November 2026 the two-year rule is still the operative law, so 18 months falls short and she cannot bring an ordinary claim. If the same dismissal instead occurred in February 2027, after the ERA 2025's threshold is scheduled to have commenced, her 18 months' service would comfortably exceed the new six-month qualifying period, and she would be able to bring a claim.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On the November 2026 facts, Aisha cannot bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim, because the current two-year qualifying period still applies and she has only 18 months' service. Had the same dismissal occurred in February 2027, after the ERA 2025's six-month threshold is scheduled to be in force, she would have enough service to claim.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that most precisely explains why the current two-year qualifying period still applies today.
testPool.passage: The Employment Rights Act 2025 received Royal Assent in 2025, but Royal Assent brings an Act onto the statute book — it does not, by itself, bring any particular provision into force. The reduction of the unfair dismissal qualifying period from two years to six months is contained in the Act, but takes effect only once the relevant commencement regulations are made, which is currently scheduled for 1 January 2027. Until that date, s 108(1) ERA 1996's existing two-year requirement remains the operative law governing any dismissal.
testPool.ratioSentence: Until that date, s 108(1) ERA 1996's existing two-year requirement remains the operative law governing any dismissal.

testPool.prompt: Two employees are each dismissed for an ordinary conduct reason after ten months' continuous service. In which scenario is an ordinary unfair dismissal claim available, on current commencement plans?
testPool.scenarioA: Employee A is dismissed on 20 December 2026, before the ERA 2025's six-month qualifying period is scheduled to commence.
testPool.scenarioB: Employee B is dismissed on 5 January 2027, after the ERA 2025's six-month qualifying period is scheduled to have commenced.
testPool.explanation: B is dismissed after the scheduled 1 January 2027 commencement date, by which point ten months' service would satisfy the new six-month threshold. A is dismissed before that date, while the current two-year requirement under s 108(1) still applies, and ten months falls well short of two years.

testPool.prompt: A zero-hours worker asks her manager in late 2026 whether she has a legal right, today, to demand guaranteed hours reflecting her regular working pattern under the Employment Rights Act 2025. What is the correct answer?
options: No — the guaranteed hours right is enacted but not yet in force; an implementation date has not been fixed and is expected during 2027
Yes — it has applied to all zero-hours workers automatically since the Act received Royal Assent
No — the right was dropped from the Act entirely before it passed
testPool.explanation: The guaranteed hours right is part of the enacted Act but, like the unfair dismissal and fire-and-rehire reforms, has not yet commenced. Its implementation date is not yet fixed and is currently expected sometime in 2027 — it was not dropped from the Act, and Royal Assent alone did not bring it into force.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the Employment Rights Act 2025 as a single event that happened all at once on Royal Assent. Check the specific provision, check its actual commencement date against the date on the facts, and remember that trade union recognition and access are the one part of this reform wave already in force — everything else covered here is still prospective law layered onto the current scheme in lessons 5–8.
